title: Stable matching: proposals, blocking pairs and stable outcomes

items.prompt: A’s best-first preference row is X W Y. What does this row say?
options: A ranks X first, W second and Y third.
A assigns X a numerical utility of 3.
X also ranks A first.
A can match only with X.

items.prompt: The right-side labels are W, X and Y. Which proposed row for A must this strict complete explorer refuse?
options: Y X W
W X W
X Y W
W Y X

items.prompt: A ranks W first and X second; B ranks X first and W second. Which conclusion follows from those rank positions alone?
options: A values W exactly twice as much as X.
A and B experience equal happiness at rank 1.
Each person’s first option is preferred to that person’s second option.
The sum of the ranks measures total welfare.

items.prompt: For a complete matching, when do an unmatched-to-each-other left participant and right participant form a blocking pair?
options: Whenever the left participant prefers the alternative.
Whenever they have the same numerical rank.
Whenever either participant has a second-choice partner.
When both strictly prefer each other to their current partners.

items.prompt: Preferences are A: W X; B: W X; W: B A; X: A B. In the matching A–W and B–X, which pair blocks?
options: B–W: both would improve from rank 2 to rank 1.
A–X: both would improve from rank 2 to rank 1.
A–W: an existing pair always blocks.
No pair blocks because everyone has a partner.

items.prompt: Keep A: W X; B: W X; W: B A; X: A B. Now inspect A–X and B–W. Is it stable?
options: No, because A has a second-choice partner.
Yes: A wants W, but W prefers the current partner B; B already has the first choice.
No, because the participants have different ranks.
Yes, because every complete matching is stable.

items.prompt: A is provisionally held by W. B next proposes to W, and W’s order puts B above A. What is the atomic decision?
options: W keeps both A and B until the next round.
W must keep A because A proposed first.
W holds B, releases A and leaves A free to propose again.
A and B are permanently rejected by W.

items.prompt: Left proposes. A: W X Y; B: W X Y; C: X W Y. W: B A C; X: A C B; Y: A B C. After A→W is held and B→W replaces A, which proposal comes next under the lowest-index free-proposer rule?
options: C→X, because C has not proposed yet.
B→X, because B must try every receiver.
A→W again, because A was released.
A→X, because A is the lowest-index free proposer and W was already tried.

items.prompt: W’s best-first order is B A C. W currently holds B and receives a proposal from C. What happens?
options: W rejects C and continues holding B.
W replaces B because C proposed more recently.
W releases B and waits for A.
C is removed from the whole problem.

items.prompt: In this strict complete equal-size model, what does proposer optimality mean for the completed deferred-acceptance result?
options: Every proposer gets the first choice in the original list.
Each proposer gets the best partner that proposer can have in any stable matching of these preferences.
The result maximizes a measured total happiness score.
The stable matching is necessarily unique.

items.prompt: Preferences are A: W X; B: X W; W: B A; X: A B. Left-proposing gives A–W/B–X; right-proposing gives A–X/B–W. The explorer finds no blocking pair in either. What does this establish?
options: One of the two stable results must be a software error.
Stability chooses the objectively fairest result.
These preferences have at least two stable outcomes, and the proposing side can select a different one.
Every possible preference profile has exactly two stable outcomes.

items.prompt: With four participants on each side, why is 16 a valid upper bound on the number of proposals in this explorer?
options: Every execution must contain exactly 16 proposals.
There are 16 complete matchings.
A receiver can hold four proposers at once.
There are 4 × 4 proposer–receiver pairs, and a proposer never repeats a receiver.
